data.reasoning: The package is a standard repackaging of an upstream .deb from the official vendor (Oray). The main binary source has a pinned SHA-256 checksum, closing the swap risk. The only unpinned source is an HTML license file fetched over HTTPS from the vendor's own documentation domain (service.oray.com); this file is not executed during build/install, so it poses no supply-chain injection risk. The PKGBUILD, .install script, systemd service, and metadata files all contain routine packaging logic with no malicious code, obfuscation, or unexpected network activity. The disagreement was caused solely by API errors (HTTP 400) in the qwen model when reviewing .SRCINFO and sunloginclient.install, not by any actual security concern.
data.disagreement_analysis: The qwen model encountered LLM API failures (HTTP 400 BadRequestError) when attempting to audit .SRCINFO and sunloginclient.install, resulting in an 'inconclusive' verdict for those files and thus the overall package. The deepseek model successfully audited all five files and correctly found them safe. The disagreement is purely a tool failure, not a substantive security disagreement.
coverage_issues: qwen model failed to review .SRCINFO and sunloginclient.install due to LLM API errors (HTTP 400), leaving 2 of 5 files unaudited
learnings: Tool errors (API failures, timeouts) should not propagate as 'inconclusive' security verdicts. The orchestration layer should retry failed file audits or fall back to another model before rendering a package-level verdict.

When a package-level verdict is blocked by tool errors on low-risk files (like .SRCINFO), the system should distinguish between 'inconclusive due to security uncertainty' and 'inconclusive due to infrastructure failure' to avoid false escalation.

Models correctly applied the threat model by not flagging a SKIP checksum on a non-executable HTML file from the vendor's own domain as a supply-chain risk, demonstrating good discrimination between packaging hygiene and actual injection vectors.
